The Houston Brass Band is a traditional British-style brass band. Directed by Houston Symphony trumpeter Robert Walp, the Houston Brass Band’s unique blend brings an exciting sound to a wide range of selections, from Elizabethan music to marches, film scores, modern compositions, as well as the classics.  Rarely found in the United States, the traditional British-style brass band is known for its unique sonority and virtuosic compositions.

With Ms. Hogg’s beautiful house as a backdrop, the Houston Brass Band will be performing at Bayou Bend Family Day on Sunday, April 17, at 3:00 pm. We will celebrate the American author, with music such as Stephen Foster’s Jeanie with the Light Brown Hair and George Gershwin’s Summertime. We will also be performing a piece of music that has not been heard in over 100 years: The Houston Light Guard March, composed by Mrs. C.A. Bujac, F.W. Schmidt, and C. Grunewald in 1896. This march honors the Houston Light Guard, which has been in existence since 1873.

All are welcome to join us at this special occasion, and admission to the Bayou Bend Collection is free.

The FREE one-day celebration will focus on the merits of mindful, sustainable living while educating and encouraging Houstonians to preserve, conserve and enhance our city and the Earth. Developed by Air Alliance Houston 3 years ago (formerly Galveston-Houston Association for Smog Prevention (GHASP) and Mothers for Clean Air), Earth Day Houston is a collaboration with the City of Houston and various green nonprofit agencies.

Planned activities include the Earth Zone featuring interactive environmental awareness activities highlighting land, air, water, and renewable energy. Urban Harvest Farmers Market will be open in support of locally-grown produce, and Green Team America will host a recycling bin art contest between Houston-area high schools. Festival guests are encouraged to visit the air, water, land, and renewable energy zones to learn about each zone. Completed passport card holders will be eligible to win tickets to several green-friendly local excursions courtesy of Green Bank.

Earth Day Houston is the city’s official Party for Our Planet held on Saturday, April 23, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Earth Day Houston celebrates a day of family entertainment, environmental education, and the Green Expo!

Filmmaker Robert Zemeckis topped his breakaway hit Romancing the Stone with Back to the Future, a joyous comedy with a dazzling hook: what would it be like to meet your parents in their youth? Billed as a special-effects comedy, the imaginative film (the top box-office smash of 1985) has staying power because of the heart behind Zemeckis and Bob Gale's script.

High schooler Marty McFly (Michael J. Fox, during the height of his TV success) is catapulted back to the '50s where he sees his parents in their teens, and accidentally changes the history of how Mom and Dad met. Filled with the humorous ideology of the '50s, filtered through the knowledge of the '80s (actor Ronald Reagan is president, ha!), the film comes off as a Twilight Zone episode written by Preston Sturges.

Filled with memorable effects and two wonderfully off-key, perfectly cast performances: Christopher Lloyd as the crazy scientist who builds the time machine (a DeLorean luxury car) and Crispin Glover as Marty's geeky dad.

title: Five Friends from Japan: Children in Japan Today
description:
Children's Museum of Houston explores culture and life through the eyes of five new Japanese friends with the exhibition Five Friends from Japan: Children in Japan Today. On view Jan. 29 - May 1, 2011. With the support of Mitsubishi.

Journey to the Land of the Rising Sun, but don’t pack your bags quite yet! Beginning, January 29, 2011, travel without a passport to the new Five Friends from Japan exhibit at the Childrens Museum of Houston (CMH). Designed to entertain by highlighting similarities and differences between Japan and the U.S., Five Friends from Japan peeks into contemporary Japanese life through individual stories of five new foreign friends. The exhibit advances understanding and appreciation of Japanese culture with true stories and real objects straight from Japan.

“Five Friends from Japan is an awesome opportunity for you to tour Japan and experience contemporary Japanese lifestyle through the five students highlighted in the exhibit,” said Bunmi Gaidi, CMH Educator in charge of the exhibit. “This is a great opportunity for children to grasp similarities and differences from a contrasting culture.”

Five young Japanese kids will take you through a mesmerizing journey to their home country. Through video messaging, each will touch on various aspects of the everyday, Japanese lifestyle: family values, food, performing arts, school and celebratory traditions. Listen and relate to their authentic stories and music.

Rooms modeled after real Japanese homes feature more in-depth video narratives and hands-on activities lead by the five friends:

  • In Sakiko’s bedroom, dress in traditional Japanese attire, check out real manga (comics), and try creating your own. An only child and owner of many pets, Sakiko highlights popular culture and points out that some Japanese girls’ bedrooms may look a lot like American ones.
  • In Ken’s tatami room, experiment with Japanese calligraphy, try out futon bedding, and learn about traditional home architecture. As the oldest of four siblings with a Japanese father and American mother, Ken shares details about his family and his love of baseball and Harry Potter.
  • In Aisa’s kitchen and tofu shop, role-playing with Japanese cuisine is on the menu. With Aisa’s help, fill up on information about the variety of foods and eating habits in Japan, and learn about traditional festivals that take place in the town where she lives.
  • In Yusuke’s yard, practice aikido moves with the help of an instructor. In the garden, you will learn that not all Japanese gardens are pristinely manicured and designed for meditation. The yard is filled with Yusuke’s bug collection and sports equipment.
  • In Shoko’s living room, listen to and create different types of Japanese music. Shoko, from an elite and culturally conservative family, shares her shell and stone collections. While hanging out, notice that Shoko’s living room looks a lot like our own here in the U.S.

Observe, distinguish and acknowledge a sufficient understanding of life in Japan. Five Friends provides you with an endless opportunity of fun and adventure. Discover diversity and a different life away from your own home country.

ABOUT CHILDREN’S MUSEUM OF HOUSTON
Winner of Nickelodeon Parents’ Picks “Best Museum in Houston 2009 & 2010” and Click2Houston’s Best “Best Museum in Houston 2010,” the Children’s Museum of Houston is a Citysearch.com’s nationwide 5-star children’s museum and one of the top two Children's Museums in the country by Child magazine. Serving more than 850,000 people annually, the Children's Museum of Houston is the highest-attended youth museum in the country for its size.

The Museum is dedicated to transforming communities through innovative, child-centered learning and offers 14 galleries of hands-on exhibits and innovative bilingual learning programs for kids ages birth to 12 years. description:
Houston companies and organizations are joining forces to encourage over 50,000 young entrepreneurs to start businesses on Lemonade Day Houston 2011. This innovative program, Lemonade Day, to be held on Sunday, May 1, is a free, community-wide program dedicated to teaching children how to start, own and operate their own business through the simple and time-honored act of building and running a lemonade stand.

All told, more than 1 million Houston youth and over 10,000 local non profit organizations will be impacted by Lemonade Day. Lemonade Day provides youth with free materials and support, thanks to local sponsors, who recognize the significant benefits of teaching youth business skills early. Imperial Sugar, as the oldest company in Texas, continues to be the leader in supporting Lemonade Day and impacting the lives of Houston youth.

“As the oldest company in Texas and a vital part of the Houston community for more than 166 years, Imperial Sugar is proud to support Lemonade Day again this year,” said John Sheptor, Chief Executive Officer of Imperial Sugar. “This innovative program is teaching valuable lessons to the future business leaders of our community. Lemonade Day is good for kids and good for business.”

“At BBVA Compass, we work for a better future for people, with education being one of the main areas of focus for our corporate responsibility initiatives. As such, we wholeheartedly support Lemonade Day, understanding the instructional education, practical experience and immediate success that children receive through it. We are thrilled to play a role in kindling the entrepreneurial interests of Houston’s future business leaders. After all, for many of us, a lemonade stand was our own first taste of business.” stated Mark Montgomery, BBVA Compass Houston City President.

Lemonade Day provides youth with many life lessons, including saving for the future, and this year BBVA Compass is the newest banking/financial institution partner. Other supporters include Spark Energy, KBR, NewQuest Properties, Capital One and Pappas Restaurants.

The best part of the program is that youth learn real life skills that teach them experiential learning by starting, owning and operating their own business, which gives them the opportunity to “spend a little, save a little and share a little,” donating a portion of their profits to a local charity of choice. After covering their expenses and paying back their investors, children are encouraged to open a youth savings account.

This year, the goal of Lemonade Day is to have 50,000 new entrepreneurs hit the streets of Houston on May 1. While Lemonade Day, originated in Houston, and is being replicated in other leading cities across the country, Houston continues to have the largest number of participants each year, thanks to our local sponsors.

“Lemonade Day is a day of learning and celebrating our future. We recognize that the success of this effort is dependent upon so many businesses and individuals in our city. We are truly honored and humbled by the support of our local sponsors who are committed corporate citizens and understand the role they play in helping develop the leaders of tomorrow,” stated Clare Sullivan, Board Chair of
Lemonade Day Houston.

Lemonade Day Houston is presented by Imperial Sugar and BBVA Compass, along with other local sponsors, including Capital One Bank(Founding sponsor of Serving Up Lemonade curriculum), Spark Energy, Holthouse Foundation for Kids, KBR, NewQuest Properties, Pappas Restaurants, Hilcorp Energy Company, Kroger, Safety Vision, Amegy Bank of Texas, Houston CPA Society, Condera Advisors, Fore Thought Financial Group, Inc., Avalon Advisors, LLC, Ergos Technology, Linbeck, Caesar Systems, PKF, Zadok Jewelers, Gill Foundation, NYMEX Foundation, IBC Bank, Senterra, MyCityRocks, Mayer Brown, Hot Shot, Sudhoff Properties, Papa John’s, Limb Design, Yaffe|Deutser, Jason’s Deli, Chinese Community News, Captivate Network, Raising Cane’s, One Green Street, and California Pizza Kitchen. Lemonade Day is also grateful for its many strategic and school district partners.

On Lemonade Day, everyone has a job – either buying or selling lemonade. Houstonians are encouraged to simply purchase a cup of lemonade from one of the youth participating in the program, to demonstrate how our community cares for the future of youth in Houston.

Lemonade Day is a part of Prepared 4 Life, a non-profit that provides fun, proactive and experiential programs infused with life skills, character education and entrepreneurship.

Lemonade Day was born in Houston in 2007, and was inspired by the lessons local entrepreneur and philanthropist Michael Holthouse taught his young daughter and her friend when they set-up a lemonade stand. Since then it has grown to a nationwide program, and this year Lemonade Day will expand to 28 cities.

To sign up or learn about ways that everyone can get involved in Lemonade Day, May 1, 2011, please visit www.LemonadeDay.org.

title: 3rd Annual Houston Family Triathlon
description:
The Jewish Community Center of Houston will be the sight of the 3rd Annual Houston Family Triathlon Sunday, May 1 from 7:30 a.m. – 11:00 a.m.

The USA-Triathlon sanctioned event is the only family event with a race for every member of the family regardless of age. The event also features a team category allowing a parent and child to combine times to compete against other parent children teams. The triathlon is three events: swimming, biking and running.

The event is being organized by the JCC in conjunction with Tri Kids Camp, a non-profit organization founded in 2007 that encourages children ages 9-16 to live an active lifestyle by introducing them to triathlon training and competitions in a safe, healthy and fun environment.

Proceeds from the triathlon benefit the JCC Meals on Wheels program and Achieve Houston, a summer camp for inner city kids that teaches the sport of triathlon, as well as proper nutrition, strength and core training and making better life choices.

Open to all age groups, the 3rd Annual Houston Family Triathlon is a unique family experience. Parents can watch children race, then race themselves. Prizes will be awarded to the top three finishers in each youth division. By design, the competition will consist of a wide variety of athletes from beginners to elite.

“With the obesity epidemic on the rise, the 3rd Annual Houston Family Triathlon hopes to play a major role in fighting inactivity. The overall goal of this event is to promote physical fitness and health in our children,” said Charles Moser, event director and founder of Tri Kids Camp and Achieve Houston.

Families with children ages 9-16 from throughout the community are encouraged to register and participate. They will compete in one of three categories: 9-12 year olds, 13-16 year olds and 17 and up. The 9-12 year olds will compete in 200 meters swim, 5K bike and a 2K run. The 13-16 year olds will compete in 300 meters swim, 10K bike and a 4K run. Adults race a challenging 400 meter swim, a fast 15K bike ride and an entertaining neighborhood 6K run. All youth participants will receive a finisher’s medal, goodie bag, post race snack and a chance to win door prizes.

Visit www.jcchouston.org  or www.trikidscamp.org  for more information about registering for the 3rd Annual JCC Houston Family Triathlon or contact Charles Moser at toothcm@peoplepc.com.

title: The Edge Continued Concert Series
venue: Ned S. Holmes Performance Hall: Lamar High School
description:
City Dance Company will take the stage at Ned S. Holmes Performance Hall in Lamar High School on Saturday, April 30, at 7:30pm and Sunday, May 1 at 3:00pm. The Edge Continued Concert Series will feature performances by both the Apprentice Company and the Professional Company. These performances will comprise of dynamic dance moves, upbeat rhythms, and innovative styles, creating an uplifting experience for everyone to enjoy.

The Edge Continued is bringing the community together once again to illustrate the performers’ dedication to reinventing themselves artistically on stage and off. They have performed a vibrant mix of jazz, hip-hop, and classical styles in theaters and at cultural events locally and internationally such as: Spain, France, Switzerland, and Monaco. These experiences have taught the Company the significance of teaching dancers about various cultures, while sharing their unique talents and style to others.

City Dance will utilize their unique assortment of age groups in the Edge Continued by incorporating performances from the City Dance Ensemble and the DanceCircle. While the City Dance Ensemble’s members are high school students, the DanceCircle is comprised of professional career women between the ages of 30-60. Together, these dancers will deliver an unforgettable performance. The audience will watch the dancers move gracefully across the stage with confidence and poise, while other pieces demonstrate lively movements with beating rhythms. Overall, the Edge Continued will push the boundaries of contemporary dance and create a unique artistic atmosphere.

Artistic Director Sherese Campbell is motivated to keeping City Dance a non-profit dance studio that “seeks to reflect the ethnic diversity of the Houston Metropolitan area.” Members from the community look forward to watching the diverse ethic, social, and cultural backgrounds come together and perform. The organization encourages students to further develop their personal character and talents through community service projects. The Company has performed for various hospitals, churches, retirement communities and schools. Through these unique opportunities, the dancers have discovered the importance of sharing their talents and utilizing their artistry in positive ways.

Tickets to the performance will be $15.00 for the general public and $10.00 for students with ID. Lamar High School is located on 3325 Westheimer Rd. in Houston, Texas. For ticket information, please call 713/529-6100. For additional information on City Dance or upcoming performances, please call 713-529-6100 or visit the website at www.houstoncitydance.com.

title: Sarah Cortez:  book signing and discussion
description:
Friday, May 6 at 6:30 p.m. Murder by the Book presents Sarah Cortez.   Anthologist/Poet Sarah Cortez has edited a book of detective/mystery stories for teens called You Don't Have a Clue.

A first anthology of suspenseful short fiction by Latinos for teens. The teens featured in these stories deal with situations typical to all young adults, including attraction to the opposite sex-or to the same sex, in one story-and first sexual encounters, problems with family and friends, academic and personal aspirations.

When two gun-toting hoodlums tell the fourteen-year-old narrator of Rene Saldana's story, "The Right Size," to kiss the floor, he doesn't think twice. And his dad and younger brother drop to the floor just as quickly. "This guy Jimmy probably thinks Dad is the greatest threat among the three of us, but he's dead wrong. Dad couldn't hurt a bug," the boy thinks. In the ensuing twenty minutes, he learns that his dad isn't as weak as he thought, and in fact, his dad is willing to do whatever it takes to protect his family, even if it means killing someone.

The teens featured in these stories deal with situations typical to all young adults, including attraction to the opposite sex--or to the same sex, in one story--and first sexual encounters, problems with family and friends, academic and personal aspirations. But they also deal with every kind of thrilling situation imaginable, from missing girls to kidnappings and dismembered bodies. A young girl finds herself living with her "family," though she has no memory of them or who they claim she is. A geek at a prestigious public high school finds himself working with his very attractive arch-rival to solve the mystery of a severed, bloody arm that appears inexplicably in his locker. And Mike's life sucks when his parents split up, but it gets worse when his best friend is abducted by a thug shot by Mike's dad, a police officer. There's something for everyone here, with aliens, ghosts and even an Aztec god making appearances in these stories.

Set in schools and communities from New York City to Venice Beach, California, the protagonists reflect the breadth and diversity of the Latino authors included in this innovative collection. Published authors such as Mario Acevedo, Alicia Gaspar de Alba, Diana Lopez and Sergio Troncoso appear alongside less well-known authors who deserve more recognition. With an introduction by young adult literature expert Dr. James Blasingame of Arizona State University, this collection is sure to keep readers on the edge of their seats until the last page is turned.

SARAH CORTEZ is a poet, educator, and law enforcement officer. She is the author of a poetry collection, How to Undress a Cop (Arte Publico Press, 2000), which won the PEN Texas Literary Award in Poetry, and the editor of Windows into My World: Latino Youth Write Their Lives (Pinata Books, 2007), winner of a 2008 Skipping Stones Honor Award; Hit List: The Best of Latino Mystery (Arte PÃºblico Press, 2009) and Indian Country Noir (Akashic Books, 2010). She lives and works in Houston, Texas. .

title: Greyson Chance & Cody Simpson (in the Bronze Peacock)
description:
House of Blues presents Greyson Chance & Cody Simpson (in the Bronze Peacock).

When 13-year-old Greyson Chance posted a clip of himself performing Lady Gaga’s “Paparazzi” on YouTube in April, he never dreamed that the video would become a viral sensation viewed by more than 28 million people. The clip, shot by Greyson’s dad, shows the Cheyenne Middle School sixth-grader at the piano, singing his heart out at a choir event as the female-dominated audience looks on slack-jawed with amazement.

Greyson’s obvious talent led to an invitation to appear on The Ellen Degeneres Show just two weeks later (his first-ever plane trip), where he chatted confidently with DeGeneres, performed “Paparazzi,” and fielded a congratulatory on-air phone call from Lady Gaga herself, who advised him to “work really hard, be focused, and stay away from girls,” adding what had already become readily apparent: “You’ve already won over everyone’s hearts.”

Indeed this bright-eyed, freckled-faced kid has become a star in just a few short months.

As a kid growing up on Australia’s sun-drenched Gold Coast, Cody Simpson (pictured above) used to watch his father play guitar and sing for friends and family at parties and backyard barbecues. Seeing how music brought people together, Cody asked for his own guitar and lessons at the age of seven. After learning a few chords from his teacher, Cody wrote his first song. “It was about putting a diaper on a chicken,” he says with a laugh. “Who knows what my seven-year-old brain was thinking?”

Cody’s parents encouraged him to keep singing and practicing his guitar. By age 12, he began posting YouTube videos of himself performing covers of songs by artists who inspired him, including Justin Timberlake, Jason Mraz, and The Jacksons.

Cody is currently in the studio working on tracks for his upcoming full length debut on Atlantic Records.

title: Kid's Play 2011: ONE
description:
Hope Stone Inc.’s Kid’s Play/YouthSound Ensemble presents Kid's Play 2011: ONE, Saturday, May 7, 2:00pm and 7:00pm, at Barnevelder Movement Arts Complex. 2201 Preston Street.

Hope Stone Dance concludes its season with its cutting-edge presentation of kid’s art entitled ONE, a one-hour production showcasing the young members of the Kid’s Play/YouthSound Ensemble. The must-see show features a fantastic array of dance, theater, music, photography and spoken word performed by 60 very talented 6- to 18-year-old students.

Kid's Play is an arts outreach project that works with children and teens of all walks of life. The program, established in 2002, believes art is a healing modality for our youth, who are at risk due to the pressures and forces society places upon our children. Master teachers and artists use dance, music, photography, theater, and yoga and work with an art ensemble of pre-teens and teens (ages 6-18) during a year-long scholarship arts residency at the Hope Center studios (1210 W. Clay, Ste. 26). The students attend classes each week, working more intensely in the artistic fields, under the guidance of their teachers. This more in-depth study and immersion in the art allows the students to create new pieces that reflect a new level of learning, positive mental health and enhanced self-esteem.

Each spring a new cutting edge kid’s performance is premiered, written by the staff but powered by the students. This performance is the culmination of the work in a nurturing and supportive performance atmosphere creates a positive boost within each child.

title: Run! Jump! Fly! Adventures in Action
description:
Children's Museum of Houston inspires kids to get physically active in 2011 with Run! Jump! Fly! Adventures in Action, January 15 - May 8, 2011. Sponsored by The Farish Fund.

Star as your own action hero! With child obesity on the rise and New Year resolutions to get fit begin, the Children’s Museum of Houston (CMH) revitalizes exercise into entertainment. Beginning Saturday, January 15, 2011, CMH combats childhood inertia with Run! Jump! Fly! Adventures in Action: an interactive exhibition featuring action-adventures popular in children’s books, movies and TV. You are invited to jump into action star training exploring kung fu, surfing, snowboarding, yoga, horizontal climbing and more—all designed to build strength, coordination, balance and endurance. The exhibit’s objective is to get you pumped about doing the things you already like to do.

“Run! Jump! Fly! gets kids moving,” said Lynnsey Dohmen, CMH Educator in charge of the exhibit. “It teaches children physical activity is fun and complements our PowerPlay exhibit nicely. It features a great snowboarding/skiing component which centers around balance—an attribute not currently showcased in PowerPlay.”

PowerPlay is a fierce, extraordinary permanent exhibit at CMH where kids track their bodies’ responses to physical challenges. PowerPlay focuses on getting kids active and making them aware exercise is fun and good for you! This will be the place where Run! Jump! Fly! will pack its punch.

While you move through the exhibit and have fun with physical activity, you will develop ideas for how to become more active daily. Throughout Run! Jump! Fly!, you stamp the activities you accomplished on Action Trackers. You can also take home Action Tracker 3-Day Missions which are activity logs encouraging you to get physically active for a total of 60 minutes a day.

READY, SET…ACTION! Run! Jump! Fly! Adventures in Action features four adventure scenes and an action star training center. Each adventure scene provides an imaginative setting in which kids can try out a high appeal physical activity and highlight a specific physical challenge of balance, strength, coordination or cardiovascular endurance.

Surfing and Snowboarding (Balance): Don Hawaiian shirts or down-style vests, choose one of four balance boards and see how long you can stay on for the ride. A motion sensor triggers a two-minute video sequence which takes you through pine trees and past lakes as you snowboard down a mountain. Then, the video takes you off the edge of a cliff and sailing into the clouds before landing as surfers in the ocean. The activity challenges and builds your balance.

Kung Fu Forest (Coordination): Enter a clearing in a bamboo forest and begin the kung fu session with a bow to show the three principles of kung fu: strength, peace and respect. Three lantern posts display instructional images of kung fu animal stances – still, “ready” positions inspired by the rooster, the snake and the tiger. After you try the animal stances, you can push a button to trigger a sequence of light box images that guide you from still poses into a flow of action. The panels also illustrate the cultural origins of kung fu and other martial arts.

Climbing Canyon (Strength): A trailhead marker introduces four different trails: the Toddler Trail, Beginners’ Bend, Rugged Ridge and the Extreme Expanse. You successfully traverse the trails to safely explore a cave holding a hidden treasure. Hand and footholds guide you across the horizontal walls. The climbing canyon shows you how lifting and holding up you own body weight is a valid strength-building activity.

Flycycle Sky (Endurance): Merge your imagination with physical activity when you strap on a bike helmet and climb on one of the Museum’s flycycles. These stationary bikes with wings or propellers each face a cloud-shaped panel. For every few rotation of the wheels, a star lights up in the sky. The flycycles vary in form: one is a tandem bike with a recumbent seat in front, an upright in back and two pairs of wings above; another is a hand-pedaled chariot with an overhead propeller.

Action Star Training (Balance, Strength, Coordination, Cardiovascular and Muscular Endurance): The action star training center provides you with challenges of balance, strength, coordination and cardiovascular and muscular endurance through simple activities that kids can do at home.

  • At the Yoga Station, try out the tree pose and the cat stretch, as well as learn the origins of yoga.
  • At the Strength Center, a kid-friendly interpretation of gym equipment, experiment with upper- and lower-body strength. You can try out monkey bars, leg presses, self-weighted rowers, and adaptive chin-ups.
  • In the Dance Club, choose dance moves and music to get your heart pumping, going freestyle or following the dancer on the screen.

Leave CMH with a better understanding of how to recognize your potential for action in daily life. Run! Jump! Fly! provides you with an endless opportunity of fun and adventure. Come out and discover how creativity and imagination can play vital roles in fun physical activity!

ABOUT CHILDREN’S MUSEUM OF HOUSTON
Winner of Nickelodeon Parents’ Picks “Best Museum in Houston 2009 & 2010,” and Click2Houston’s Best “Best Museum in Houston 2010,” the Children’s Museum of Houston is a Citysearch.com’s nationwide 5-star children’s museum and one of the top two Children's Museums in the country by Child magazine. Serving more than 850,000 people annually, the Children's Museum of Houston is the highest-attended youth museum in the country for its size.

The Museum is dedicated to transforming communities through innovative, child-centered learning and offers 14 galleries of hands-on exhibits and innovative bilingual learning programs for kids ages birth to 12 years. The Children’s Museum operates as a 501(c)(3) under the direction of a Board of Directors and is located at 1500 Binz in Houston’s Museum District. Admission is $8 per person and $7 for seniors 65 years and older and for members of the military. Children under one and Museum Members receive free admission.

McGovern, M.D. Hours are Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Thursday from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sunday from Noon to 6 p.m. The Museum is open at 9 a.m. on the Second Saturday of every month for Museum Members. The Museum is closed Mondays but open on Federal Holidays, during Houston Independent School District’s Spring Break and during the summer months from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

A little bit of History:
The beginnings of the Greek Orthodox community in Webster, TX began in 1993 with a small but growing Greek community.

We began the Greek Festival as a way to share our culture and heritage with our neighbors. At the Festival our neighbors can sample our food, our culture and visit our church see the awe inspiring Byzantine iconography. This three day festival takes the combined efforts of everyone in the church. The Ladies, young and old, will cook for weeks on end to get the pastries done just right. The men will build the infrastructures for the festival and also cook. Everybody works even the children!

The Greeks at one time had conquered the known world and excelled in philosophy, arts and medicine. They were also one of the first to accept Christ. The bible was written in Greek and the liturgy or service that was developed 2000 years ago is still practiced at St. John the Theologian Greek Orthodox Church every Sunday in Webster. As you can guess we are proud of our church and our heritage and we welcome you!

title: Alley Theatre Young Performers Studio (Saturdays)
description:
The Alley Theatre presents the Young Performers Studio (YPS), Saturday Studios ages 8-15, Saturdays, October 2, 2010 – May 14, 2011 , 10:00AM -11:30AM.

Young Performers Saturday Studios are process classes that teach students how to do theatre. Basic skills such as acting, writing, directing, voice, movement, and improvisation will be taught on a continuing basis with students constantly being challenged to expand their skill set. Occasional sharing sessions will be scheduled as students achieve certain benchmarks, but the focus will be less on performance and more on becoming better artists of the theatre.

Since classes will be ongoing, it will allow us to bring in specialty teachers to teach units on specific teaching methods. Such units will include: Viola Spolin’s Theatre Games, Rasa Boxes, Anne Bogart’s Viewpoints and Laban Movement techniques. Schedules will be released monthly and students will be able to choose which classes interest them most.

There is an annual family membership fee of $30 to become a member of the Young Performers Saturday Studio. A Flexcard must be purchased in order to attend a Saturday Studio session at the Alley Theatre.

We offer 24 studio classes during the school year. There are many options for each student within the following age groups and skill levels.

  • •Basic (ages 8-10)
  • •Scene Lab (ages 8-10)
  • •Fundamentals (ages 11-15)
  • •Troupe (ages 11-15)
  • •Vanguard (ages 10-15)

The Flexcard allows families the grace to attend classes when it is convenient. Each time a class is taken, the Flex card will be stamped. All students will be evaluated at the start the 2010/11 season for placement purposes. Advancement to a different level will be determined after three sessions by teaching artists as key skills and benchmarks are demonstrated. This is a great program for students involved in other theatre and performing arts programs.

The YPS Flexcards cost $120 for 8 classes or $70 for 4 classes.

All punch cards expire on May 14, 2011 or 6 months after being purchased.

All classes are Saturday from 10:00am-11:30am. The 2010-2011 dates are:

  • •February 5, 12 & 19
  • •March 5 & 26

title: Dora & Diego’s 4-D Adventure: Catch that Robot Butterfly!
description:
Moody Gardens 4D Special FX Theater presents  Dora & Diego’s 4-D Adventure: Catch that Robot Butterfly!

Beginning Mar. 12, Moody Gardens will present Dora & Diego’s 4-D Adventure, a new family friendly theatrical film and attraction based on Nickelodeon’s hit animated preschool series Dora the Explorer and Go, Diego, Go!. For the first time ever, families can see these popular characters animated in digital 3-D, with special effects that make the story burst off the screen. To kick off the new attraction, Dora and Diego will make special appearances at Moody Gardens on the opening day of the film.

In Dora & Diego’s 4-D Adventure, visitors will join Dora, Diego and Boots as they travel from the tropical rainforest to the icy Arctic in a high-speed chase to protect the world’s animals from Swiper’s newest invention—a Robot Butterfly!

Moody Gardens’ 4-D theater combines the visual drama of a 3-D film with a variety of sensory effects that are built into the seats and theater environment, bringing on-screen images to life with added effects such as water mist, a neck air blast, snow, bubbles, leg ticklers, scents, enhanced floor lighting, and seat vibrations.

The 4-D Theater is included on the Moody Gardens Day Pass ($39.95 adults and children), which includes one admission to all Moody Gardens attractions for one day. Single tickets to the 4D Theater are also available for $10.95 (adults) and $8.95 (children). Tickets may be purchased on-site or at www.moodygardens.org.

This year marks Dora the Explorer’s 10th anniversary, which Nickelodeon will celebrate throughout the year with “Beyond the Backpack” – a multiplatform pro-social campaign that champions overall school readiness for preschoolers; four prime-time Dora-themed television specials; an original documentary directed by Academy Award®-nominated Brett Morgen; and a dedicated website www.DoratheExplorer.com.

Dora & Diego’s 4-D Adventure was produced by SimEx-Iwerks and Super 78. SimEx-Iwerks is the leading innovator of immersive 3-D and 4-D Attractions and the exclusive distributor of the industry’s best selling film titles. The company supports over 150 family-friendly attractions in more than 30 countries. Super 78 Studios is a group of artists and technicians who have consistently delivered entertaining and educational stories across all platforms. For over 12 years, the award winning creative and production company continues to help extend well-known brands and intellectual properties into special venues and the experiential market.

Nickelodeon, now in its 31st year, is the number-one entertainment brand for kids. It has built a diverse, global business by putting kids first in everything it does. The company includes television programming and production in the United States and around the world, plus consumer products, online, recreation, books, and feature films. Nickelodeon's U.S. television network is seen in more than 100 million households and has been the number-one-rated basic cable network for 16 consecutive years.

For more information or artwork, visit www.nickpress.com. Nickelodeon and all related titles, characters and logos are trademarks of Viacom Inc. (NYSE: VIA - News, VIA.B - News).

Moody Gardens is a public, non-profit educational destination utilizing nature in the advancement of rehabilitation, conservation, recreation and research. For more information on Moody Gardens visit www.moodygardens.org.

title: EcoTrackers (Ages 9-12): Magnificent Metamorphosis
description:
The Houston Arboretum & Nature Center presents EcoTrackers.  

EcoTracker classes inspire young naturalists - ages 9 to 12 - to explore their surroundings and deepen their knowledge of the natural world. All classes include a short introduction inside followed by outdoor activities. The majority of class time is spent outside incorporating hands-on, engaging activities. Participants should come dressed for the weather, wear closed toe shoes, and bring a snack and water.

Programs are held one Saturday a month from September to May. Parents are welcome to drop their kids off or to stay and participate with their child.

Spring 2011 Schedule:
This spring, come and learn about insects and other creepy crawlies!

Beetle Mania - January 15: 9:00-11:00 a.m.
Beetles are the group of insects with the largest known number of species. Discover some beetles with interesting adaptations. Investigate the darkling beetle and take home your own darkling beetle larva.

Colony Dwellers - February 19: 9:00-11:00 a.m.
Ants have a social structure within their colonies. Explore how each job is essential to the community and how important communication is.

Detritivores: Dead Leaves for Lunch - March 26: 9:00-11:00 a.m.
Organisms such as millipedes and termites help the decomposition process by eating dead plant material. Explore the ecosystem of a rotting log and learn how dead plants are turned into new soil.

Pint-sized Predators - April 16: 9:00-11:00 a.m.
Not all predators are large animals. Even insects have their share of predators among them. Investigate predators such as praying mantis and dragonflies and find out how they help the ecosystem.

Magnificent Metamorphosis - May 21: 9:00-11:00 a.m.
Butterflies go through metamorphosis. Search for butterflies at different stages of their life cycles and learn how to attract butterflies to your backyard.

title: Faces of Houston
description:
The Children's Museum of Houston (CMH) invites Houston’s children to be a part of the art and to realize that every race and every face make up an integral part of a cohesive whole. A collection of 100,000 digital photos of Houston’s own youth will form a majestic picture mosaic to line the museum’s block-long Kid’s Hall and applaud the city’s vast variety in cultures. This exhibition, titled Faces of Houston, opens February 5, 2011.

This unique montage of fused photographs depicts the beauty of diversity while metaphorically highlighting every child’s role as an individual as well as a community member. By displaying photos of Houston’s children, the Museum hopes to inspire everyone to appreciate the value of cultural diversity that makes up our community and expand the walls of a common playground

“The world lives in Houston,” said CMH educator Bunmi Gaidi, who’s in charge of the project. “Faces of Houston seeks to instill in children tolerance and curiosity; to show them we’re the same inside but unique outside.”

This visually immersive experience will encourage families to stand back from the murals to make out kids’ faces, or move closer to take an intimate look at the individual images that make up the mosaic. Faces of Houston will be an artistic expression of beauty where the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

A PICTURE SPEAKS A THOUSAND PICTURES
The entire length of Kid’s Hall will welcome families with nine larger-than-life photographic mosaics of children who embody Houston’s diversity. Each image will be eight feet tall, made up of a combination of 100,000 one-inch by one-inch photos (each selected by CMH from a wide range of partners.)

The nine kids prominently displayed in the mosaics will be children who have been impacted by CMH’s programming and reflect the city’s mix of races and cultures. Their headshots taken by astounding photographer Everett Taasevigen.

ABOUT EVERETT TAASEVIGEN
California native, Everett Taasevigen, is no stranger to the Bayou City. Having traveled on assignments to Houston since 1996, he was captivated by the city’s art scene and decided to move here permanently last year. He worked as the lead photographer for California’s high-tech, new media festival, 01SJ. His list of photographed high profiles include renowned Florentine artist, Gianni Cacciarini. He most recently shot with ZenFilms during the grand opening of the Lee and Joe Jamail Skatepark, and has partenered with the ART GUYS’ Jack Massing, on several projects.

ABOUT CHILDREN’S MUSEUM OF HOUSTON
Winner of Nickelodeon Parents’ Picks “Best Museum in Houston 2009 & 2010” and Click2Houston’s Best “Best Museum in Houston 2010,” the Children’s Museum of Houston is a Citysearch.com’s nationwide 5-star children’s museum and one of the top two Children's Museums in the country by Child magazine. Serving more than 850,000 people annually, the Children's Museum of Houston is the highest-attended youth museum in the country for its size. The Museum is dedicated to transforming communities through innovative, child-centered learning and offers 14 galleries of hands-on exhibits and innovative bilingual learning programs for kids ages birth to 12 years.

The Children’s Museum operates as a 501(c)(3) under the direction of a Board of Directors and is located at 1500 Binz in Houston’s Museum District. Admission is $8 per person and $7 for seniors 65 years and older and for members of the military. Children under one and Museum Members receive free admission.

Free Family Nights are offered Thursdays from 5 to 8 p.m. courtesy of The Wortham Foundation, Inc. and Kathrine McGovern and the late John P. McGovern, M.D. Hours are Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Thursday from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sunday from Noon to 6 p.m. The Museum is open at 9 a.m. on the Second Saturday of every month for Museum Members. The Museum is closed Mondays but open on Federal Holidays, during Houston Independent School District’s Spring Break and during the summer months from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. For more information, please visit www.cmhouston.org  or call (713) 522-1138.

title: Houston Symphony at CWMP:  Star-Spangled Salute
description:
CELEBRATE THE ARTS! A world-renowned symphony and ballet, gifted musicians from around the world, award-winning children’s performers…it’s all in your own backyard at The Cynthia Woods Mitchell Pavilion’s 2011 Performing Arts Season.

This season encompasses a journey filled with classical music, dancing, tributes to late, great musicians, patriotic fanfare, Italian pop and more. The season features eight exhilarating performances by the Houston Symphony. The Texas Music Festival Orchestra returns to the stage along with Houston Ballet for a mixed-repertory program. 

Sunday, July 3
Star-Spangled Salute
Houston Symphony -  Michael Krajewski, (pictured) conductor
8 p.m. / Gates open at 6:30 p.m.
Free event generously presented by The Woodlands Development Company.

The Cynthia Woods Mitchell Pavilion dons red, white and blue July 3 for the return of the Star-Spangled Salute. This free Independence Eve spectacular features the Houston Symphony in a selection of patriotic favorites.

Led by Principal Pops Conductor Michael Krajewski, the Symphony performs a variety of traditional favorites, American classics, sing-alongs, and of course, Tchaikovsky’s “1812 Overture” complete with cannons from atop the hill.

Don’t miss commemorating the birth of our nation by joining the Symphony in this grandiose celebration. It’s an evening of good, old-fashioned family fun!

Pre-concert activities begin at 6:30 p.m.

The Pavilion offers these extraordinary performances for no cost with free mezzanine and lawn seating for all Houston Symphony concerts and Houston Ballet’s performance, as well as free seating at the Star-Spangled Salute and Texas Music Festival Orchestra.

Plus, picnics are welcome at all performing arts events. Bring your family to The Pavilion in 2011 and celebrate the arts!

description:
Delight in the magical land of scarecrows and pumpkins during the annual Scarecrow Festival, October 8-9 in the historic town of Chappell Hill.  The Scarecrow Festival boasts more than 300 juried exhibitors showing their wares such as home decor, holiday items, artisans, clothing, jewelry, gardening, and so much more.

title: CYBERCHASE - The Chase is On!
description:
It is the classic good vs. evil adventure! Hacker, a power-hungry villain, is on a mission to take over Cyberspace. Now, it is up to three curious kids and a cyberbird to use their wits and smarts to save the Cyberworld!

Join forces with the CyberSquad: Matt, Inez, Jackie and Digit, in an original quest to save Cyberspace! Blast off into CYBERCHASE – The Chase Is On!, an out-of-this-world, math adventure opening in the Children's Museum of Houston’s (CMH) new building on March 14, 2009.

One of seven new expansion exhibits, CYBERCHASE – The Chase Is On! is an exciting addition to the Museum’s permanent exhibits! Based on CYBERCHASE™, the Emmy award-winning PBS KIDS GO! math mystery cartoon, CYBERCHASE – The Chase Is On! presents math in a fun, kid-friendly environment, allowing children to make use of their critical thinking skills and approach math with an investigative, positive attitude.

In the exhibit, children will enter Cyberspace through a special portal to explore favorite cybersites, including Control Central, the Grim Wreaker and Poddleville, and be greeted by Motherboard, the peace-loving leader of Cyberspace. They will help the CyberSquad protect the virtual universe from the evil Hacker while exploring math concepts such as place value, algebra, geometry, fractions and probability.

FEELING GOOD ABOUT MATH  “Recent studies show students’ math skills drop further as they go up to the next grade level,” said Vanessa Chenault, CMH project manager. Experts attribute this pattern to the lack of opportunities for kids to develop critical thinking skills and apply what they learn in school to real world contexts. “This affects their overall confidence and attitude towards math. Then, they grow up thinking they are not good at math, so they stay away from it,” added Chenault. “Math is a universal language. Understanding it becomes imperative as we lean more toward complicated global technologies.”

CYBERCHASE – The Chase Is On! will provide children with those opportunities to develop a fascination of math. Throughout the exhibit’s adventurous plots, children will not only “do” math, but will be able to experience it firsthand through the many activities and interactive components. They will strive to solve challenges as they learn how to apply assorted mathematical concepts in non-threatening, exciting contexts, enhancing their problem-solving skills in the process.

¡COMIENZA LA AVENTURA! In addition to addressing a need for mathematical experiences in informal settings, CYBERCHASE – The Chase Is On! will provide materials for museums and science centers to reach out to the growing Hispanic population across the country. Both English and Spanish speaking families will gain a variety of mathematical skills that apply to their real life, in addition to a renewed confidence and interest in mathematics.

title: Invention Convention
description:
Step into a workshop of gadgets and gizmos where kids create, concoct and construct contraptions at Invention Convention, an exhibit where kids use their creativity and imagination to become inventors! Kids will experience the processes involved in the act of invention and ingenuity. They will dream-up and design in a workshop filled with half-finished contraptions, bins of spare parts, drafting tables, schematics and various instruments from floor to ceiling!

One of seven new permanent expansion exhibits, Invention Convention opens in the Children’s Museum of Houston’s (CMH) new wing on March 14, 2009. With more than 3,000 square feet of exhibit space, Invention Convention provides an opportunity for children to apply their knowledge and understanding creatively through the invention challenges provided. By working to solve these open-ended challenges, they develop a better understanding of the science and math behind the challenges and improve their problem-solving and critical thinking skills.

“Schools today focus on making sure our children have the basic knowledge necessary to pass standardized tests. Yet, the process of simply acquiring knowledge is insufficient,” said Keith Ostfeld, CMH director of exhibit development. “Research shows children, who have the opportunity to test and apply the knowledge they are learning, not only better understand the information given to them but better utilize that knowledge to solve problems in unfamiliar situations.”

BRIGHT BRAINS, BRILLIANT BRAINPOWER Invention Convention is an event, a community and a workshop featuring self-directed, interactive activities and opportunities merging the boundaries of science, engineering, robotics and art. It allows the casual visitor to be immersed in the invention culture and mindset and encourages children to explore the processes of inventing and creative problem-solving. It becomes the place where Houston’s young inventors, tinkerers, and creators come to dream, make, test, share ideas and be rewarded.

The entire exhibit is 85 percent modular and can be moved around as needed to meet specific needs, highlight a particular activity or allow for special events. More than just an outlet for creative energies, Invention Convention is a program and a support network for young people interested in invention and engineering! They can freely share ideas and get advice as a mutual-interest community. Children will find themselves “tinkering” around as they experiment with gadgets and gizmos like LEGO® bricks, propellers, magnets, batteries, switches and buzzers through facilitated, hands-on experiments and mini-workshops.

They will have the opportunity to work on projects, such as building a jitterbug, designing rubber band powered cars, or assembling burglar alarms. “If we, as Americans, want to remain on the global cutting-edge for technological and other advances, we must encourage our children to be more than just knowledgeable,” said Ostfeld. “Like all the great inventors, they must be able to creatively apply said knowledge to define and solve problems and remain stalwart in their resolve to find solutions in the face of failure. Invention Convention is a venue where creativity flows, experimentation is encouraged and failure is celebrated as much as success—a place to help grow America’s future inventors and engineers.”

title: FlowWorks
description:
Fierce forces will run wild and it will be up to you to tame them! Harness the power of water as FlowWorks bursts from the floodgates of your imagination into reality at the Children's Museum of Houston (CMH).

The first of seven new permanent exhibits in CMH’s expanded new building; FlowWorks makes a splash in the bigger and better Allen Family Courtyard, flushing visitors with a sip of excitement! With 4,000 square feet of exhibit space and more than 30 hands-on experiences, it unleashes a tsunami of wet, wild fun! This state-of-the-art exhibit dives into the forces and properties of water through currents, vortices and rapids, exploring the fascinating concept of fluid dynamics!

“FlowWorks is a visitor-driven experience of experimentation and exploration dependent upon how you, as the visitor, engage in the activities with other visitors,” said Keith Ostfeld, Director of Exhibit Development at CMH. “It’s a totally unique entity where you have the potential to have a different experience every time you visit.” Water’s physical properties come to life as a variety of natural phenomena. Dip your hands in and watch how whirlpools and rapids stir up. Harness water’s power through lock systems, boat building and dams, and examine methods to store, release and manipulate water’s energy.

GO WITH THE FLOW From the big splash when a gargantuan cauldron empties into a reservoir 18 feet below, to the free-standing exhibit pieces, FlowWorks is off the hook! It provides children with hands-on opportunities, which focus on the concepts of energy transformation through the medium of water. They examine how water’s power and pressure is controlled and the force it exerts. The activities are constructed, so kids do not have to enter the water except with their hands or tools.

“Many of the physics principles relating to fluid dynamics are difficult concepts for children to understand because of its abstract nature,” said Ostfeld. “In fact, many adults dedicate their lives to the study of it. But, underlying the complexity is an inherent, fascinating beauty. By using water as a medium for children to explore the concepts, they become researchers in their own right, studying the major governing principles and getting to glimpse the awe-inspiring complexity of the movement of fluids.”

Dams, paddle wheels and such, connect to the flowing water system and are each influenced by manipulating certain variables like pressure, volume, and shape. Navigate an aqueduct maze or fill the huge cauldron using squirts, Archimedes screws and bucket lifting devices! Feel the rush of waters through a simulated flood plain or serve as the mastermind behind a hydro switchboard. Find out what dams are for, how electricity is created and how objects respond to water!

“Few other museums have tried to tackle so many different aspects of water’s properties and uses in one single exhibit, let alone through some of the very dramatic interactives,” said Ostfeld. “We’ve managed to pour it all into one exhibit. Kids are going to jump overboard with excitement!”

title: Kidtropolis, USA
description:
It’s a city for kids, run by kids! Kidtropolis, USA marks a brand new spot on the map as a real-life kid metropolis complete with a skyline, city government, occupations and the systems which make a city work. It’s where kids can choose to be whatever they want to be! This exhibit engages children and their families in financial literacy and civic engagement.

One of seven new, permanent, state-of-the-art expansion exhibits, Kidtropolis’ city gates open in the Children's Museum of Houston’s (CMH) new wing on March 14, 2009.

“When visitors enter Kidtropolis, USA, they will feel as if they have just walked into a real, authentic city,” said Christina McKee, CMH project manager and exhibit developer. “It’s an exhibit which empowers children to make their own ‘grownup’ choices. They decide what issues matter the most to them.”

Kids will keep the city running by taking on the roles of city leaders, voters, workers, shoppers and business owners. With more than 4,700 square feet of exhibit space, they will participate in a sophisticated, simulated economy where they can spend money on items and experiences throughout. But, like in real life, they will have to get jobs to earn money.

“In the face of a recession and credit crisis, it is now more important than ever to help children and their families understand the fundamentals of finances and economics,” said McKee. “Kidtropolis will provide an immersive environment where kids make their own social and financial decisions and witness the immediate consequences of their actions. We want them to be successful in life, but those skills have to be acquired and put to practice at an early age.”

PROUD TO BE A KIDTROPLIAN Upon entering the Museum, children will receive their own KidCard—a debit card which has a stipend of 60 Kidtropolis Dollars on it. With it, they can go on a shopping spree of tantalizing food items, special art workshops and other cool stuff. But once they spend it all, it’s gone! They can prevent financial loss by getting jobs as bankers, commodities traders, diner or market employees, police detectives, EMTs, dispatchers, city planners, city council members, journalists, veterinarians, artists, and much more! In fact, there are more than two dozen jobs in Kidtropolis, USA.

Each gig has a not too shabby salary wage of 20 Kidtropolis Dollars. They can deposit their paychecks into a savings or checking account or hit the town for a day out. Kidtropolis mirrors a real city, complete with its own city hall, municipal building, mercantile center, bank, news center, market, diner, art school and even a vet clinic! These set of iconic buildings line the main strip of the flourishing metropolis. But, the city only comes to life once its citizens begin to “live” in it and enjoy all it has to offer! Kids will witness how a city is dependent upon its people and the services they provide to each other.

BE ALL YOU CAN BE “It is important children learn they can make a difference in their community,” said McKee. “As a citizen, it is your job to know the issues affecting your community and express your opinion. One of the best ways to do this is by voting.” Children can make their voice count and engage in civic duties by voting and electing a mayor, campaigning for city council office, passing city ordinances, voicing their opinions about upcoming ballots, voting on city council referendums and participating in dynamic debates.

They also can play the role of detective to solve crimes plaguing the city, be dispatchers and inform police about emergencies, or even play cop. They can decide how Kidtropolis should spend its money, manage their own money, and buy and sell stocks. They can promote city happening’s by anchoring the news, work as veterinarian and treat and diagnose animals, or explore their talents working as artists. “A lot of kids say: ‘This is what I want to be when I grow up,’” said McKee. “But in Kidtropolis, you don’t have to wait to be a grownup to be all you can be.”

title: Matter Factory
description:
It’s the stuff too small to see, but too big to ignore! By the time our kids become adults, they will more than likely be immersed in a new industrial revolution – a science focusing on the super small! One of seven new, cutting-edge, permanent expansion exhibits, Matter Factory takes a closer look at materials science and nanotechnology and debuts on March 14, 2009. It is the result of a partnership with Rice University’s Education Center for Biological and Environmental Nanotechnology (CBEN) and the University of Houston’s Smart Materials and Structures Laboratory.

Step into a whimsical factory and stare straight into the future! The Children's Museum of Houston’s (CMH) Matter Factory gives visitors a glimpse into the concepts of materials science, including properties of matter and potential uses for different substances and smart materials. With 1,350 square feet of exhibit space, children explore how matter matters in our daily lives. They experiment with different matter properties; test and sort materials based on their properties, and examine unique properties of emerging materials recently developed by scientists.

“Matter is everywhere! Matter Factory is a multi-sensory exhibit that encourages kids to investigate and explore the unusual and exciting stuff we touch, smell, see, and hear every day,” said Keith Ostfeld, CMH director of exhibit development.

WHAT’S THE NANO WITH YOU? CMH is one of few informal education centers in the entire country to take on the challenge of presenting nanotechnology—this often complex, yet important subject matter! CMH is excited to be one of the few informal education centers to bring it to an elementary audience. Matter Factory provides a foundational understanding of this tiny technology, including exploring the extreme smallness of the nano-scale, the properties of materials at the nano-scale, and how scientists conduct research at the nano-scale.

“Nanotechnology and smart materials are the science of our future,” said Ostfeld. “From more durable cell phones to buildings which can resist earthquake tremors, nanotechnologists and material scientists have already developed products to help improve our lives. Matter Factory increases awareness of this promising new science and encourages kids to recognize its potential.” Kids also will develop an understanding that everything is made up of matter. They will learn that molecules and atoms are the building blocks of matter as they investigate materials and solve “factory” problems. They will test the invisible properties of matter discovering the density, conductivity and viscosity of different materials. They will interact with what scientists call “smart” materials – materials which have properties that can be dramatically changed!

“Smart materials and nanotechnology are at the apex of current advances in chemistry and materials science,” said Ostfeld. “Children need to have a solid grounding in understanding matter, the properties of matter, materials science and an introduction to both smart materials and nanotechnology if they are to compete, function or become an integral part of this new scientific revolution.”

title: PowerPlay
description:
Leap, jump, crawl and climb up the Children's Museum of Houston’s (CMH) mighty new exhibit PowerPlay. This fierce, extraordinary exhibit is an innovative and interactive approach to children’s health and physical education, where kids track their bodies’ responses to physical challenges. PowerPlay focuses on getting kids active and making them aware exercise is fun and good for you!

It is the result of a partnership with Baylor College of Medicine, made possible by a Science Education Partnership Award from the National Center of Research Resources (NCRR).  PowerPlay packs a powerful punch in the Museum’s new building as one of its seven new, permanent, state-of-the-art expansion exhibits opening March 14, 2009.

“PowerPlay is an adrenaline rushed experience, which turns familiar physical activities and presents them in an exciting new way to get kids moving,” said Tara Lang, CMH project manager of expansion exhibit development. “They’ll be surprised to find getting healthy is easy and fun because play is one of the greatest forms of exercise!” With more than 4,700 square feet of exhibit space, kids will work up a sweat in more than a dozen action-packed components. They will become researchers tracking their fitness by doing what they already do: play! They can climb, jump, dance, race and stretch! Then, play an active role in determining and understanding their physical abilities by measuring their bodies’ response to fitness.

“The U.S. health education is reaching a crisis point. Studies show there’s an epidemic of childhood obesity. The nation’s chronic killers, heart disease and stroke, cancer and diabetes, are linked to health habits established in youth,” said Lang. “PowerPlay engages children and their families in inquiry-based investigations that promote understanding, positive attitudes and healthy behaviors related to physical activity, diet, and the effects of physical activity on the human body.”

I’VE GOT THE POWER Power Trackers found throughout the exhibit’s three levels will allow children to record their measurements, rate their experiences and compare their physical performances online. This unique central feature of the exhibit is a computerized tracking system that enables them to document data at activities throughout the three floors.

Using KidCards, they register information over multiple visits. Kids log in, take their baseline heart rates at check stations and print activity logs when they exit. When they go home, they can view their activity logs on the kid-friendly PowerPlay web site (accessed via cmhouston.org/powerplay ), complete extra activities, add data and get information about healthy living! “It’s about taking control of your life and making sound decisions about how to live it,” said Lang. “They can use these records to track their improvement. They can perform at-home physical challenges and enter their results online. Teachers can even use the suggested curriculum and conduct classroom explorations linked to the online database before and after a school field trip.”

Children can run through a climbing and crawling course, capture images of their own bodies in action, or discover new and fun ways to incorporate exercise into their daily lives. They also can measure their grip strength, follow along different dance moves, or race around an interactive game board while increasing their speed and heart rate! Kids can meet real scientists and researchers from Baylor College of Medicine, learn about their work and participate in facilitated workshops at the Power Science Lab! But the highlight of the exhibit is the 35 feet tall, three-story high iconic Power Tower, which spans through all exhibit levels. Comprised of six integrated towers, this 1,200 square foot monumental climbing structure serves as the visual core of PowerPlay. With its avant-garde lily pad steps and five miles of connecting steel aircraft cables, the exhibit’s premise of play, power and potential comes to life! “This is a high-tech health exhibit like none other,” said Lang. “It will grow with each child and help them gain lifelong tools to assess their health and make active lifestyle choices.”

title: Tot*Spot
description:
As early as infancy, children learn about their world and the people who live in it. Because they have a natural curiosity about their environment, they benefit from free exploration and open-ended discovery. However, there aren’t many places in the city which focus solely on stimulating and developing their skills.

On March 14, 2009, that’s all about to change because the Children's Museum of Houston (CMH) is opening its doors to a brand new Tot*Spot—an entire exhibit level just for infants and toddlers! This kid-friendly, bilingual exhibit will give tots, from birth to age three, the opportunity for exploration, discovery, experimentation and wonder within distinct areas designed to develop critical thinking, problem solving and motor skills.

One of seven new expansion exhibits, Tot*Spot will be exclusively located on the second floor of the Museum’s new wing. With over 3,400 square feet of exhibit space, it will offer a range of activity zones organized by age and activity type.

“Tot*Spot is a wonderful setting that enhances parents’ knowledge of their child, the importance of play and gives them ideas of activities, which can be replicated at home,” said Christie Shaw, Tot*Spot educator. “By giving infants and toddlers opportunities to explore, we enable them to learn about themselves and the environment around them.”

AN EXCLUSIVE FLOOR JUST FOR TOTS Tot*Spot is more than just a nice place for infants and toddlers to play. It is a total learning environment where every child is engaged in problem-solving and idea discovering. It is a fun-filled wonderland of invigorating activities complete with a stroller alley for easy stroller parking. Families are isolated in their own exclusive floor away from the crowds. They don’t have to worry about germs because the exhibit is cleaned every two hours. In fact, no shoes are allowed in Tot*Spot, but shoe covers are provided. From the entry pergola, families get a 180 degree view of the exhibit and can spot where they want to start their joyous journey.

Studies suggest 85 percent of a child’s brain has already developed by age three, so it is crucial they get every advantage at an early age to become a healthy, successful adult later in life. Tot*Spot will enable children to develop their motor, cognitive, multi-sensory and verbal skills through countless hands-on activities. They will learn through a variety of ways: whole body experiences; their senses; exploration, observation and repetition; cause and effect experiences; and interaction with others. Tots will tinker with tot-friendly gadgets, meander along whimsical paths, climb in and out of oversized windows and doors, and experiment with multi-colored dash lights.

But, they will not be the only benefactors of the expanded exhibit. To help stimulate their growth at home, the Museum will have activity sheets available for parents as well as parenting resources at the Museum’s Parent Resource Library, a branch of the Houston Public Library, where local educators will routinely be available to offer their expertise on child development and growth.

title: Lady Gaga
description:
Toyota Center presents Lady Gaga.   Due to overwhelming demand, Lady Gaga will play a THIRD show at Toyota Center on Friday, April 8, 2011!

Lady Gaga has captivated audiences around the globe with her stunning international smash, The Monster Ball tour. With the majority of the 2010 North American dates already sold out, Lady Gaga, joined by Semi Precious Weapons, announced she will return to North America in 2011. In keeping with her flair for the theatrical, as well as her innovative and creative spirit, the show promises to push the limits of the live concert experience, bringing fans a spectacle even more eye-popping than what they experienced during the thrilling first leg of The Monster Ball.

When Lady Gaga was a little girl, she would sing along on her mini plastic tape recorder to Michael Jackson and Cyndi Lauper hits and get twirled in the air in daddy’s arms to the sounds of the Rolling Stones and the Beatles. The precocious child would dance around the table at fancy Upper West Side restaurants using the breadsticks as a baton. And, she would innocently greet a new babysitter in nothing but her birthday suit.

It’s no wonder that little girl from a good Italian New York family, turned into the exhibitionist, multi-talented singer-songwriter with a flair for theatrics that she is today: Lady Gaga.

“I was always an entertainer. I was a ham as a little girl and I’m a ham today,” says Lady Gaga, 23, who made a name for herself on the Lower East Side club scene with the infectious dance-pop party song “Beautiful Dirty Rich,” and wild, theatrical, and often tongue-in-cheek “shock art” performances where Gaga – who designs and makes many of her stage outfits -- would strip down to her hand-crafted hot pants and bikini top, light cans of hairspray on fire, and strike a pose as a disco ball lowered from the ceiling to the orchestral sounds of A Clockwork Orange.

“I always loved rock and pop and theater. When I discovered Queen and David Bowie is when it really came together for me and I realized I could do all three,” says Gaga, who nicked her name from Queen’s song “Radio Gaga” and who cites rock star girlfriends, Peggy Bundy, and Donatella Versace as her fashion icons. “I look at those artists as icons in art. It’s not just about the music. It’s about the performance, the attitude, the look; it’s everything. And, that is where I live as an artist and that is what I want to accomplish.”

That goal might seem lofty, but consider the artist: Gaga is the girl who at age 4 learned piano by ear. By age 13, she had written her first piano ballad. At 14, she played open mike nights at clubs such as New York’s the Bitter End by night and was teased for her quirky, eccentric style by her Convent of the Sacred Heart School (the Manhattan private school Nicky and Paris Hilton attended) classmates by day. At age 17, she became was one of 20 kids in the world to get early admission to Tisch School of the Arts at NYU. Signed by her 20th birthday and writing songs for other artists (such as the Pussycat Dolls, and has been asked to write for a series of Interscope artists) before her debut album was even released, Lady Gaga has earned the right to reach for the sky.

“My goal as an artist is to funnel a pop record to a world in a very interesting way,” says Gaga, who wrote all of her lyrics, all of her melodies, and played most of the synth work on her album, The Fame (Streamline/KonLive/Cherrytree/Interscope). “I almost want to trick people into hanging with something that is really cool with a pop song. It’s almost like the spoonful of sugar and I’m the medicine.”

On The Fame, it’s as if Gaga took two parts dance-pop, one part electro-pop, and one part rock with a splash of disco and burlesque and generously poured it into the figurative martini glasses of the world in an effort to get everyone drunk with her Fame. “The Fame is about how anyone can feel famous,” she explains. “Pop culture is art. It doesn’t make you cool to hate pop culture, so I embraced it and you hear it all over The Fame. But, it’s a sharable fame. I want to invite you all to the party. I want people to feel a part of this lifestyle.”

The CD’s opener and first single, “Just Dance,” gets the dance floor rocking with it’s “fun, L.A., celebratory vibe.” As for the equally catchy, “Boys Boys Boys,” Gaga doesn’t mind wearing her influences on her sleeve. “I wanted to write the female version of Motley Crue’s ‘Girls Girls Girls,’ but with my own twist. I wanted to write a pop song that rockers would like.”

“Beautiful Dirty Rich” sums up her time of self-discovery, living in the Lower East Side and dabbling in drugs and the party scene. “That time, and that song, was just me trying to figure things out,” says Gaga. “Once I grabbed the reigns of my artistry, I fell in love with that more than I did with the party life.” On first listen, “Paparazzi” might come off as a love song to cameras, and in all honestly, Gaga jokes “on one level it IS about wooing the paparazzi and wanting fame. But, it’s not to be taken completely seriously. It’s about everyone’s obsession with that idea. But, it’s also about wanting a guy to love you and the struggle of whether you can have success or love or both.”

Gaga shows her passion for love songs on such softer tracks as the Queen-influenced “Brown Eyes” and the sweet kiss-off break-up song “Nothing I can Say (eh eh).” “‘Brown Eyes’ is the most vulnerable song on the album,” she explains. “‘Eh Eh’ is my simple pop song about finding someone new and breaking up with the old boyfriend.”

For the new tour for this album, fans will be treated to a more polished version of what they saw (and loved) at her critically acclaimed Lollapalooza show in August 2007 and Winter Music Conference performance in March 2008. “This new show is the couture version of my handmade downtown performance of the past few years. It’s more fine-tuned, but some of my favorite elements to my past shows – the disco balls, hot pants, sequin, and stilettos – will still be there. Just more fierce and more of a conceptual show with a vision for pop performance art.”

It’s been a while since a new pop artist has made her way in the music industry the old-fashioned/grass roots way by paying her dues with seedy club gigs and self-promotion. This is one rising pop star who hasn’t been plucked from a model casting call, born into a famous family, won a reality TV singing contest, or emerged from a teen cable TV sitcom. “I did this the way you are supposed to. I played every club in New York City and I bombed in every club and then killed it in every club and I found myself as an artist. I learned how to survive as an artist, get real, and how to fail and then figure out who I was as singer and performer. And, I worked hard.”

Gaga adds with a wink in her eye, “And, now, I’m just trying to change the world one sequin at a time.”

Don’t miss your chance to see Lady Gaga LIVE at Toyota Center in April!
